props.title: Hair
props.initialSlug: Free spirits fight war & conformity in Vietnam era

sections.content: Hair revolutionized the movie musical by capturing the raw energy of 1960s counterculture through Milos Forman's kinetic direction. Unlike traditional stage-to-screen adaptations like West Side Story (1961), Hair embraced a naturalistic, documentary-like approach while maintaining its theatrical roots. The film's opening sequence, with Treat Williams' Berger disrupting Central Park with "Age of Aquarius," immediately establishes its rebellious spirit. Forman, fresh off One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest (1975), brought his outsider's perspective to this distinctly American story of protest, freedom, and generational divide.

sections.content: The film's treatment of the Vietnam War draft stands in stark contrast to later, more direct war films like Platoon (1986) or Full Metal Jacket (1987). Instead, Hair uses music and dance as metaphors for resistance and social change. The "White Boys/Black Boys" sequence brilliantly tackles racial inequality through provocative musical staging, while "Walking in Space" creates a hallucinatory commentary on war and peace that influenced later surreal musicals like Pink Floyd The Wall (1982).

Choreographer Twyla Tharp's contribution cannot be overstated. Her blend of modern dance, ballet, and street movement created a new language for film musicals, influencing everything from Fame (1980) to Moulin Rouge! (2001). The Central Park dance sequences, particularly during "Aquarius," demonstrate how cinema can transform stage choreography into something uniquely cinematic. SUBHEAD: Cultural Impact and Legacy

sections.content: While Hair wasn't an immediate box office success, its influence on film musicals is undeniable. The movie helped bridge the gap between traditional Hollywood musicals like The Sound of Music (1965) and more experimental fare like Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975). Its frank treatment of sexuality, drug use, and political protest paved the way for modern movie musicals that tackle serious themes, from Rent (2005) to Les Misérables (2012).
